content: Larrea tridentata, commonly known as the creosote bush, is a flowering plant in the family Zygophyllaceae. It is also referred to as chaparral when used as a medicinal herb and is called gobernadora in Mexico, which translates to governess, due to its ability to dominate water resources by inhibiting the growth of nearby plants. In the Sonoran region, it is more commonly known as hediondilla. The species is named after Juan Antonio Hernandez de Larrea, a Spanish clergyman. The creosote bush thrives in well-drained soils, particularly on alluvial fans and flats. In some areas, it forms nearly pure stands, although it is often found in association with Ambrosia dumosa (commonly known as burro bush or bur-sage). Interestingly, the roots of the creosote bush produce chemicals that inhibit the growth of burro bush roots, though the exact nature of their relationship remains unclear. These chemicals, however, do not fully explain the regular spacing observed between individual plants within a stand. The even distribution of plants in a creosote bush stand resembles a man-made orchard. Initially, it was believed that the plant released water-soluble inhibitors to prevent the growth of other bushes nearby. However, it is now understood that the root systems of mature creosote plants are so efficient at absorbing water that seeds falling nearby cannot gather enough moisture to germinate, creating dead zones around each plant. Additionally, all plants within a stand appear to grow at a similar rate, and the creosote bush is known for its remarkable longevity. Young creosote bushes are highly vulnerable to drought stress compared to established plants. Germination occurs actively during wet periods, but most young plants die quickly unless optimal water conditions are present. Ground heat exacerbates their susceptibility to water stress, with soil temperatures reaching as high as 70°C (160°F). For a young plant to become established, it must experience three to five years of unusually cool and moist weather during and after germination. This suggests that all plants within a stand are of the same age. Mature creosote bushes, however, are highly drought-tolerant. They can function at water potentials as low as -50 bars and have been found surviving at levels as low as -120 bars, although the practical limit is around -70 bars, where the plant's need for cellular respiration exceeds the capacity of photosynthesis to provide energy. During periods of water stress, cell division can still occur, and new cells rapidly absorb water after rainfall, causing branches to grow several centimeters at the end of a dry season. Water loss is minimized by the resinous, waxy coating on the leaves and their small size, which prevents them from heating above air temperature and thus reduces vapor pressure deficits. While the plant sheds some leaves in preparation for summer, complete defoliation is fatal. Fallen leaves and other debris trapped by the canopy create a unique ecological community, supporting organisms such as beetles, millipedes, pocket mice, and kangaroo rats. Larrea tridentata has been used extensively in traditional medicine by Native Americans in the Southwest to treat various conditions, including sexually transmitted diseases, tuberculosis, chickenpox, dysmenorrhea, and snakebites. The shrub remains widely used as a medicinal remedy in Mexico and contains nordihydroguaiaretic acid (NDGA). However, its use as an herbal supplement, often referred to as chaparral, has raised safety concerns. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued warnings about the health risks of ingesting chaparral or using it internally, discouraging its use. Similarly, in 2005, Health Canada advised consumers to avoid using Larrea species leaves due to the risk of liver and kidney damage. In literature and popular culture, the creosote bush has been referenced in various works. In Mary Hunter Austin's book The Land of Little Rain, the desert of Death Valley is described as beginning with the creosote bush. In Frank Herbert's science fiction series Dune, the Fremen inhabitants of the planet Arrakis use the juices of the creosote bush to prevent water loss through their skin. The name King Creosote is also the nickname of an independent singer-songwriter from Fife, Scotland. Additionally, in the 2005 film Kingdom of Heaven, Orlando Bloom's character Balian remarks, A spark and a creosote bush, there is your Moses, there is your religion, suggesting that the burning bush in the Bible may have been a simple creosote bush ignited by a spark.
